title: Contracts on Methods
story: You've built a BankAccount struct with a balance. But anyone with access to the struct can set balance to -500 — that makes no sense! You want to attach rules to the struct itself: 'You can only withdraw if you have enough money.' With XIOM, you can add `requires:` directly to methods on structs, making the struct guard its own data.
why: Attaching contracts to struct methods encapsulates validation rules with the data they protect — the struct becomes self-guarding, impossible to put into an invalid state from outside.
analogy: A struct method with a contract is like a hotel room safe. The safe (struct) has a keypad (method) with rules: 'You can only open me if you enter the correct code (requires: code is valid).' The safe ENFORCES its own rules — you can't bypass the keypad and just grab the contents. Similarly, `BankAccount.withdraw` enforces its own rules: 'You can only withdraw if you have enough money.' The struct guards itself; callers can't cheat.
try_it: Add a `deposit` method to BankAccount with `requires: amount > 0.0;` and `ensures: result > self.balance;`. Create an account with 0 balance and deposit 100, then withdraw 40. What happens if you call withdraw(-10)? The amount > 0 requires should trap. Add a `transfer` method that takes another BankAccount and an amount — with requires checking the sender has enough funds. What contracts should `transfer` have? Add `ensures: sender.result == sender.balance - amount;` style ensures (you may need to return a tuple).
tips: Use `self` in method contracts to reference the struct's fields — `self.balance`, `self.health`
Method contracts run in order: first the caller's code, then the method's requires, then the body, then ensures
Methods with contracts make invalid states unrepresentable — you CAN'T create a situation where balance < 0 through normal method calls
common_mistakes: Forgetting that `self` in a method contract refers to the struct BEFORE the method body runs, not after
Writing contracts that depend on mutable state that could change between the requires check and body execution (in multi-threaded contexts)
Expecting `self` to be updated inside ensures — `ensures: self.balance == 0;` checks the ORIGINAL balance, not the returned value
